promptText: What is the average-case time complexity of a lookup in a JavaScript Map or plain object?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
explanation: A well-distributed hash-based structure like Map gives O(1) average-case lookup, which is why turning a repeated linear search into a map/set lookup is the classic optimization pattern.

promptText: Why is `Array.prototype.shift()` O(n) instead of O(1)?
options: Removing the first element requires re-indexing every remaining element in the array
shift() internally creates and discards a full copy of the array each call
shift() is actually O(1); only unshift() is O(n)
JavaScript engines execute shift() on a separate background thread
explanation: Removing from the front shifts every other element's index down by one, making shift() (and unshift()) O(n); this is why using shift() in a loop hides an O(n^2) queue implementation.

promptText: What is the time and space complexity of the sliding-window solution to "longest substring without repeating characters"?
options: O(n) time, O(k) space
O(n^2) time, O(1) space
O(2^n) time, O(n) space
O(n log n) time, O(n) space
explanation: Each character is added and removed from the window at most once, giving O(n) time overall, with O(k) space for the map tracking characters currently in the window (k = alphabet size).

options: The default comparator coerces elements to strings and sorts them lexicographically unless you pass a numeric comparator
sort() is broken for arrays containing more than two elements
sort() only works correctly on arrays of strings, never numbers
The array must be pre-sorted before calling sort() for correct results
explanation: Without a comparator, sort() converts elements to strings and compares them lexicographically, so "10" sorts before "2"; always pass `(a, b) => a - b` for numeric sorting.

promptText: Which data structure is the natural fit for validating whether a string of brackets is balanced?
options: A stack (LIFO)
A queue (FIFO)
A hash map
A binary search tree
explanation: Brackets nest last-in-first-out — the most recently opened bracket must be the first to close — which is exactly the behavior a stack provides.

promptText: What is the key advantage of memoized (top-down) or tabulated (bottom-up) Fibonacci over naive recursion?
options: It avoids recomputing overlapping subproblems, dropping time complexity from O(2^n) to O(n)
It requires writing less code overall
It only works correctly for even values of n
It removes the need for a base case in the recursion
explanation: Naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems exponentially; memoization or tabulation computes each subproblem exactly once, which is the core idea behind dynamic programming.

promptText: Why does `nums.reduce((acc, n) => (n > 0 ? [...acc, n*2] : acc), [])` silently become O(n^2) despite looking like a single pass?
options: The spread `[...acc, n*2]` copies the entire accumulator array on every single iteration
reduce() is inherently O(n^2) in the JavaScript specification
Ternary expressions inside reduce always introduce a hidden nested loop
It is actually O(n); there is no real performance issue here
explanation: Spreading the accumulator into a new array on every call copies all previously accumulated elements each time, turning an apparently linear reduce into a quadratic operation; using `acc.push(...)` instead keeps it O(n).

promptText: In the Two Sum problem, what technique improves the solution from O(n^2) to O(n)?
options: Using a hash map to check, for each number, whether its complement has already been seen in a single pass
Sorting the array first and always returning its two smallest elements
Using recursion to enumerate every possible pair of indices
Using two nested for-loops with an early-exit condition
explanation: Reframing the problem as "have I already seen the value that would complete this pair" lets a Map give O(1) lookups, so a single pass through the array suffices instead of a nested-loop comparison of every pair.

promptText: Why can't `[...str].reverse().join("")` fully guarantee a correct Unicode-safe reversal?
options: Spread iterates by code point, but it can still mishandle combining marks and ZWJ emoji sequences that form one visual grapheme from multiple code points
Spread syntax does not work on strings at all in JavaScript
reverse() only operates correctly on arrays containing numbers
join("") strips out all non-ASCII characters from the result
explanation: Spreading a string iterates by Unicode code point (fixing the surrogate-pair problem of split("")), but a grapheme like a combining-mark sequence or a ZWJ emoji spans multiple code points, so a truly correct reversal needs Intl.Segmenter.

promptText: What correctness guard does the sliding-window "longest substring without repeating characters" algorithm need, and what bug does omitting it cause?
options: Checking that the duplicate character's last-seen index is >= the current left pointer before moving left; omitting it lets a stale index outside the current window incorrectly move left backwards
Checking that the input string's length is even; omitting it causes an infinite loop
Checking that every character is lowercase; omitting it throws a runtime exception
No guard is actually needed; the straightforward version is already fully correct
explanation: Without the `>= left` check, a character's last-seen index from before the current window could incorrectly move the left pointer backwards, breaking the invariant that the window never contains a duplicate.

promptText: Why does a hand-rolled deep-clone function need a WeakMap of already-cloned objects ("seen"), while `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` makes no such attempt?
options: The WeakMap detects circular references so cloning doesn't infinite-loop; JSON.stringify has no such mechanism and simply throws on circular structures
The WeakMap exists purely to improve performance, not for correctness
JSON.stringify natively supports circular references without any extra handling
Using a WeakMap is mandated by the JavaScript spec for every recursive function
explanation: A circular reference would send naive recursion into an infinite loop; tracking already-cloned objects in a WeakMap lets the clone return the existing copy instead, while JSON.stringify simply throws when it hits a cycle.

promptText: Why is an iterative, explicit-stack version of a recursive tree/array-flattening function considered the more production-safe choice?
options: Deeply nested input can exceed the call stack's depth limit with pure recursion, throwing "Maximum call stack size exceeded," which an explicit stack avoids
Iterative versions are always asymptotically faster (better Big-O) than the recursive equivalent
Recursion is fundamentally unable to process arrays, only plain objects
JavaScript disables recursive function calls in production builds
explanation: Both versions are typically O(n), but recursion consumes call-stack frames per level of nesting; converting to an explicit stack on the heap avoids blowing the (much smaller) call stack on deeply nested real-world input.

promptText: A candidate implements `groupAnagrams` using `[...word].sort().join("")` as the map key, giving O(n * k log k) time for n words of length k. What alternative key construction improves this to O(n * k), and why?
options: Building a fixed-length character-frequency key (e.g., a 26-slot count array) avoids the per-word sort, since counting characters is O(k)
Using each word's length as the key, since anagrams always share the same length
Reversing each word before hashing, since anagram groups are structurally palindromic
Using only the first and last character of each word as the key
explanation: Sorting each word costs O(k log k); a character-frequency signature (counting occurrences of each letter) captures the same "same multiset of letters" property in O(k), dropping the total to O(n * k).

promptText: A React component creates `const debounced = debounce(fn, 300)` fresh in the component body on every render, then wires it to an input's `onChange`. What bug results, and why?
options: A new debounced closure (with a fresh internal timer variable) is created on every render, so the pending timeout from a previous render is never the one actually being tracked, meaning calls never coalesce as intended — it must be stabilized with useMemo/useRef
The bug is that debounce always fires immediately regardless of the configured wait time
This bug can only occur in class components, never in function components
There is no bug; recreating the debounced function on every render is the recommended pattern
explanation: debounce's closure over a `timer` variable only coalesces calls made through the same function instance; recreating it every render effectively resets the timer each keystroke, breaking the intended debouncing and typically requiring useMemo/useRef to stabilize.

promptText: Comparing an LRU cache built on a JavaScript Map versus one built on a plain object with manual index-tracking, why does the Map-based approach achieve O(1) get/set with eviction while staying simple?
options: Map preserves insertion order natively, so deleting and re-inserting a key on access moves it to the "most recent" end, and the first key via `.keys().next().value` is always the least-recently-used one to evict
Map automatically evicts old entries once a size limit is configured as a constructor option
Plain objects are actually faster for this use case; Map is used only for type-safety
Map and plain objects provide identical iteration-order guarantees, so there is no real difference
explanation: Map's guaranteed insertion-order iteration means the oldest untouched key is always at the front; delete-then-set on access moves a key to the back, giving linked-list-like recency ordering without hand-building one.
